gap: No result ChatGPT got says that a wrist optical sensor is the weak point for lifting and for tattooed wrists: a 2026 peer-reviewed study found 'poor accuracy during various resistance exercises' against a Polar H10 chest strap, and Garmin's support text says tattoo ink 'can block the heart rate sensor's light'. None of them says the fix is a tracker that accepts a chest strap, as Garmin's vívoactive 6 manual states it does, or one worn on the upper arm.
standout_why: I read Android Authority (rank 1, not cited) on 2026-11-17. It never mentions tattoos, wrist flexion or lifting accuracy. It brings up chest straps only as the benchmark in its Forerunner 970 test, and mentions HR broadcasting on the Xiaomi Band 10. I could not open the two cited pages: WebFetch refused wired.com and menshealth.com, and curl was not permitted. Tom's Guide came back truncated. So I can't rule out that WIRED or Men's Health mention it. ChatGPT's own answer calls the vívoactive 6 'excellent for gym training' and the Charge 6 'great for everyday fitness' without saying wrist HR is weak for lifting. That is why the score is 2, not 3.
decides: For a man buying mainly for weightlifting or gym work, or one with wrist tattoos, the wrist sensor alone is the weak link. That favours trackers that can take a chest strap (the vívoactive 6 manual says it uses chest-strap data whenever one is connected) or that are worn on the upper arm (the Amazfit Helio Strap and WHOOP 5.0 are screenless bands; our page cites the5krunner on Helio upper-arm accuracy). It counts against relying on a wrist-only band like the Charge 6 for lifting HR. For runners and daily step and sleep tracking the pick stays as it is.

findings.label: Accepts a chest heart-rate strap and uses it in place of the wrist sensor
findings.value: Manual: 'The watch is also compatible with chest heart rate monitors.' 'If both wrist-based heart rate and chest heart rate data are available when you start an activity, your watch uses the chest heart rate data.'
findings.source_title: Garmin vívoactive 6 Owner's Manual: Wrist Heart Rate
findings.note: Garmin's own US manual. The chest strap takes over automatically; no setting to change per activity.

findings.label: Wrist sensor needs the watch to stay still on the arm
findings.value: Manual: 'For more accurate heart rate readings, the watch should not shift while running or exercising.' Wear it 'above your wrist bone', snug but comfortable
findings.source_title: Garmin vívoactive 6 Owner's Manual: Wearing the Watch
findings.note: The optical sensor is on the back of the watch. The manual's 'Tips for Erratic Heart Rate Data' page (GUID-08BC6CE7…) covers lotion, sunscreen, a 5–10 minute warm-up and cold weather, but does not mention tattoos.

findings.label: Wrist optical HR accuracy during resistance training against a chest strap
findings.value: 'Both devices had poor accuracy during various resistance exercises' (Polar Ignite and Garmin Vivoactive 4S against a Polar H10 chest strap; 29 participants, 15 men and 14 women; five resistance exercises plus rest and treadmill at 5/8/10 km/h)
findings.source_title: Aydın et al., 'Can You Trust Your Wrist Heart Rate When Exercising? A Validation Study of the Polar Ignite and the Garmin Vivoactive 4S', Physical Activity and Health 10(1):107–116, published 2026-07-24
findings.note: The abstract gives qualitative results only; the open page shows no MAPE, bias or ICC numbers. At rest both devices agreed well with the H10. For walking and running the Polar agreed well and the Garmin did not. This is the older Vivoactive 4S, not the vívoactive 6.

findings.label: Tattoo ink blocks the optical sensor (Garmin's wording, as quoted by Engadget)
findings.value: 'Tattoos (ink, pattern, saturation) can block the heart rate sensor's light, causing inaccurate or missing readings.' 'For best performance, wear the watch on skin that is free of tattoos if possible.'
findings.source_title: Engadget, Cheyenne MacDonald, 'Do fitness trackers still work if you have tattoos?' (2026-06-19)
findings.note: Engadget is quoting Garmin's support FAQ at support.garmin.com/en-IE/?faq=xQwjQjzUew4BF1GYcusE59. I could not open that FAQ myself (HTTP 403). Engadget names a chest strap as the workaround 'if you don't have chest tattoos'.

findings.label: What the top uncited result says on this point
findings.value: Android Authority (rank 1) mentions chest straps only as the benchmark for its Forerunner 970 test ('heart-rate data stayed consistent with chest-strap benchmarks'). It says nothing about tattoos, lifting accuracy or connecting an external strap to its picks.
findings.source_title: I've tested all of the best fitness trackers of 2026: These are my top picks
findings.note: Its picks: Fitbit Charge 6, Garmin Venu 4, Pixel Watch 4, Apple Watch Series 11, Galaxy Watch 8, Xiaomi Smart Band 10, Forerunner 970, Huawei Watch Ultimate 2.
